searches.purpose: Re-adjudicate identity_history for an ACT-specific independent scholarly account rather than another ACBS self-description. Selected the official Cambridge Core abstract and bibliographic page for Cullen 2008: a Keele University/NHS clinician's peer-reviewed article that explicitly outlines ACT's development, identifies it as a newer contextualist and third-wave behaviour therapy, and describes the RFT-to-ACT relationship. Cambridge requires purchase or login for the article body, so only the openly readable official abstract page is cached and it is not treated as full text; a CiteSeerX PDF mirror with no clear redistribution basis was not used. Zettle's ERIC history and Hayes's PubMed third-wave article were excluded as founding-lineage accounts rather than independent historiography. The PubMed review of the third-wave metaphor, the PMC historical review of CBT, and the restricted UCL chapter were excluded because their multi-therapy framing cannot substitute for ACT-specific identity history; the PMC browser endpoint also displayed a reCAPTCHA checking shell. RFT-only scholarship, generic third-wave CBT, DBT, MBCT, MBSR, REBT, constructivist psychotherapy, cognitive-behavioral therapy as a whole, commercial ACT coaching, apps, self-help workbooks, and training-provider promotion were not counted as ACT identity evidence.

items.title: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT): A Third Wave Behaviour Therapy (abstract record)
items.rights_note: Official Cambridge University Press abstract and bibliographic page for a peer-reviewed article by a Keele University/NHS clinician, not an ACBS organizational self-description or a founding-author account. The abstract directly identifies ACT as a newer contextualist behaviour therapy, states that the article outlines its development, and describes the relationship between RFT and ACT; the keywords and issue placement also identify third-wave and contextual-therapy historiography. Cambridge marks the article body as purchase- or login-dependent, so the cached page is an abstract record only and is not treated as full text; no access control was bypassed, and a CiteSeerX PDF mirror with unclear redistribution authorization was not retained. RFT-only material cannot establish ACT identity, and generic third-wave CBT or adjacent DBT, MBCT, MBSR, REBT, constructivist-psychotherapy, and cognitive-behavioral-therapy sources cannot stand in for ACT. Commercial coaching, apps, self-help workbooks, and training-provider promotion were also excluded.

items.title: Component and Process Analysis of Cognitive Therapy
items.rights_note: Official ACBS publication record and abstract for the early comprehensive-distancing trial; not the later six-process ACT model.

items.title: About Acceptance and Commitment Therapy
items.rights_note: Professional association description; evidence of current framing and continuation, not independent efficacy evidence.

items.title: The effect of acceptance and commitment therapy on the psychological flexibility and inflexibility of undergraduate students
items.rights_note: Open process-focused meta-analysis limited to undergraduates; does not establish a universal mechanism.

items.title: Effect of acceptance and commitment therapy for depressive disorders: a meta-analysis
items.rights_note: Open disorder-specific synthesis; heterogeneity and control conditions bound conclusions.

items.title: The Effects of Internet-Based Acceptance and Commitment Therapy on Process Measures
items.rights_note: Open synthesis of internet ACT process measures; modality-specific and not interchangeable with therapist-delivered ACT.

items.title: Efficacy of Internet-Based Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for Depressive Symptoms, Anxiety, Stress, Psychological Distress, and Quality of Life
items.rights_note: Open outcome synthesis restricted to internet-delivered ACT; active- and passive-control results must remain separate.
